deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (my dating, inferred): this is an observing journal from Gauss's new meridian circle at Göttingen. The previous page has Sat 25, Sun 26, and this page has Mon 27. Together with the sidereal times of Sirius, Pollux, Spica and Arcturus, this fits Sunday 26 March 1820, the first season of the Reichenbach meridian circle. Each star line gives three clock (sidereal) wire transits | middle wire | last wire, then || the nominal circle reading followed by the micrometer-microscope readings (seconds parts of three microscopes). Barometer is in Paris inches and lines (27z 5l 55 = 27 in 5.55 lines); thermometer is in Réaumur.

(A) STAR TABLE, night of 26/27 March. Lines:
- alpha Cas at 12h30m clock: lower culmination, circle near 72°45'.
- Polaris at 12h55m38.3s: lower culmination, near 40°0', read on two wires, 2nd and 3rd 'Faden'.
- Spica: 61°52'18".
- Two faint stars of 7th and 8th magnitude ('7r Gr', '8'), near 61°45', 'cca 13' nördl.' (about 13' north).
- Arcturus: 31°32'57.5".

The readings contain an index offset of roughly 10-12' (cf. next page, zero points of the microscopes 0°8'25" etc.). Rough check with phi≈51°32': z(Spica)=phi-delta≈61°40', z(Arcturus)≈31°20', z(alpha Cas, lower)=180°-phi-delta≈73°. These are consistent up to that offset.

(B) 'Polarstern': latitude from the lower culmination of Polaris.
1. Left column, three microscope seconds 44.6, 44.6, 48.4: mean 45.87, giving 40°6'45.87".
2. Add refraction 47.80", giving z_l = 40°7'33.67".
3. Second set 44.2, 40.3, 45.3: mean 43.27; plus 47.80 gives 40°7'31.07".
4. Mean of the two sets: 40°7'32.37".
5. Combined with the value 'Lib. vom 27' (level of the 27th), 40°7'31.04": final mean 40°7'31.70".
6. With the mean 40°7'33.67" Gauss computes 40°7'33.67" + delta(88°20'10.61") = 128°27'44.28".
7. Since z_l = 180° - phi - delta, phi = 180° - 128°27'44.28" = 51°32'15.72" (double bar = result).

Refraction check: mean refraction ≈57.7" tan z ≈48.5", reduced by about 0.98×0.985 for pressure and temperature, gives ≈47". So 47.80" is plausible.

(C) Monday 27, level (Libelle), bubble end inside/outside: means 9'8.3", 3'31.85", 3'14.35" for the three microscopes (my reading). These are the level-referred zero readings.

(D) Polaris, upper culmination (daytime), observed off the meridian at clock 0h48m15s and 1h5m20s. Circle 36°40' with microscope readings:
- 1'57.0", 1'19.9", 1'2.7"
- 1'54.6", 1'18.4", 1'0.7"
Barometer 27z5l9, +11.0°R.

'Red. auf Culm.' (reduction to the meridian): +3.15" for the first observation and +4.96" for the second. This is the standard Delta z = cos(phi)cos(delta)/sin(z) · 2sin^2(t/2)/sin1".
Corrected readings:
- 2'0.15", 1'23.09", 1'5.85"
- 1'59.56", 1'23.36", 1'5.66"

For each microscope (mine, verified numerically): level reading minus mean star reading.
- Microscope 1: 9'8.30 - 1'59.855 = 7'8.445, written 7'8.45.
- Microscopes 2 and 3 have a constant 5' zero difference:
  - 3'31.85 - 1'23.225 + 5' = 7'8.625, written 8.62.
  - 3'14.35 - 1'5.755 + 5' = 7'8.595, written 8.59.
- Mean 7'8.553, so z = 36°47'8.55".

Refraction 42.30" computed logarithmically: log(43.28) = 1.63629 (mean refraction), log barometric factor 9.99207 (≈27.49/28), log thermometric factor 9.99800. Sum 1.62636, i.e. 42.30".
Apparent zenith distance z_u = 36°47'50.85".

Consistency (mine): z_u should be delta - phi = 36°47'54.9" with the latitude above. The 4" difference reflects index/flexure; Gauss does not combine the two culminations on this page. Combined, they would give phi = 90° - (z_l+z_u)/2 ≈ 51°32'18.7".
errors: Row 1, middle microscope: 1'19.9" + 3.15" = 1'23.05", but 1'23.09" is written. The 0.04" slip is negligible, or the raw reading was 1'19.94".

The reductions to culmination (3.15", 4.96") have the right magnitude. However, with the formula using phi=51°32', delta=88°20', z=36°47' and an assumed culmination about 0h55m50s clock, I get about 3.3" and 5.2". The exact hour angles Gauss used cannot be confirmed from the page; possible small discrepancy, not certain.

No arithmetic error in the latitude computation (40°7'33.67" + 88°20'10.61" = 128°27'44.28"; 180° minus this = 51°32'15.72"). The result is about 28" larger than the accepted Göttingen latitude (≈51°31'48"), because instrumental index/flexure corrections are not yet applied. This is a systematic error of the provisional reduction, not a slip.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine observing-journal page from Gauss's 1820 meridian-circle work: transit times, microscope readings, refraction, reduction to meridian, and a provisional latitude. All of it is standard astronomical practice, and Gauss's Göttingen latitude work is well known.

checkable.asserts: Order of magnitude of the reduction to meridian (≈3") for Polaris about 7.4 min from culmination

transcription_corrections: Red. auf Culm., first row, third microscope: read 1'5"85, not 1'3"85. This is confirmed by 1'2"7 + 3"15 = 1'5"85 and by the resulting 7'8"59.
'27 fd' / '37 fd' in the Polaris line is probably '2r Fd' / '3r Fd' (2nd/3rd wire, 'Faden'), not the number 27/37.
'7r Gr' = '7r Gr.' (star of 7th magnitude, 'Größe'); '8' likewise means an 8th-magnitude star.
In the Polarstern block, '−40.6.44.2' has the '40' overwritten; the small '−3.3', '−3.1' entries are marginal differences.
'Polaris' in the Montag section appears written as 'Polaris' with an abbreviated ending; the clock time reads 1h5'20": (colon = uncertain).
